reason: The moon's unique patchwork appearance and massive geological features provide a high-interest, mind-bending narrative with strong source consensus.
story: When NASA's Voyager 2 reached Uranus in 1986, scientists expected the moon Miranda to be a boring, frozen orb. Instead, they discovered a 'Frankenstein' world that looked like it was smashed to bits and glued back together by a toddler. This cosmic patchwork features mismatched geological blocks that make no sense sitting next to each other. Miranda boasts Verona Rupes, a cliff so massive it is 12 times deeper than Earth's Grand Canyon. One leading theory suggests the moon was completely shattered by catastrophic impacts up to five times, with the pieces reassembling into a chaotic pile of ice and rock. Because Uranus orbits on its side, Miranda endures extreme 42-year seasons of total darkness or constant light. We have only ever seen its southern half; the rest remains a mystery. This tiny moon, with a surface area barely larger than Texas, remains the solar system's weirdest jigsaw puzzle.
angle: Miranda features the solar system's highest cliff, a staggering 12-mile-high drop that is 12 times deeper than the Grand Canyon.

claims.claim: Miranda is the smallest and innermost of the five major moons of Uranus.
The moon was discovered in 1948 by astronomer Gerard Kuiper.
Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have provided close-up images of Miranda.
Miranda's appearance has been described as a 'Frankenstein' monster or patchwork of mismatched parts.
The moon features Verona Rupes, which is potentially the highest cliff in the solar system.
Miranda has giant canyons reaching depths of approximately 12 miles or 20 kilometers.
The canyons on Miranda are roughly 12 times deeper than the Grand Canyon.
Scientists theorize the moon may have been shattered into pieces and reassembled multiple times.
Miranda's total surface area is roughly equal to the size of Texas.
The moon contains three unique 'coronae' named Arden, Elsinore, and Inverness.
Only the southern hemisphere of Miranda has been photographed.
Miranda features a prominent V-shaped geological structure known as the 'chevron'.
The moon is likely composed of about 60 percent water ice and 40 percent silicate rock.
Because Uranus orbits on its side, Miranda experiences extreme 42-year long seasonal cycles.
Miranda is tidally locked to Uranus, meaning it always shows the same face to its planet.
The moon's orbital inclination is unusually high for a body so close to its planet.
Miranda's geological activity was likely powered by tidal heating from its gravitational relationship with Uranus.
Miranda is named after a character from William Shakespeare's play The Tempest.

disputed: Height of Verona Rupes: Sources vary wildly, ranging from 3 miles (S7) to 12 miles (S3, S6); S1 provides both 12 miles and 3-6 miles in different sections. The script should use 'up to 12 miles' or attribute the height as an estimate.

Formation of the coronae: Some sources favor the 'shattered and reassembled' theory (S1, S2, S3), while newer studies favor tidal heating and ice upwelling (S1, S5, S6, S7). The script should present both as competing scientific hypotheses.
